legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y1/Session 6/Seton Hall/Case Study_ Seton Hall.docx, plus NCAA Basketball Team Statistics.xlsx) frames a live NCAA selection-committee vote on Seton Hall's tournament seeding. Verified via WebSearch that the underlying data workbook is real 2019-20 Division I season data (353 teams; Seton Hall 21-9, Big East, matches Wikipedia and shupirates.com; Kansas 28-3 No.1 overall composite, Auburn 25-6 SEC, Virginia 23-7 with an elite defensive rating -- all consistent with independently verifiable 2019-20 facts). Critical finding NOT in the legacy source: the actual 2019-20 NCAA Tournament was canceled outright on March 12, 2020 due to COVID-19 -- no bracket, seed list, or committee vote was ever finalized or made public. The legacy case's live-vote framing describes an event that did not actually happen. Rather than silently keep a fictional frame dressed as fact, case.md's Background discloses this plainly and reframes the case as an explicit reconstruction: real, dated data from the day the season stopped, asking the question the real committee never finished answering. The specific 5-5 tie / roll-call scene in the Overview is disclosed as a dramatized frame, not a documented vote (committee internal deliberations are never made public by rule). Two real rankings that did exist on that date -- the final AP media poll (No. 15) and the NCAA's own NET ranking (No. 15, corrected 2026-08-18 from an earlier-cited No. 12 mid-season value -- see sources[] S5) -- were sourced and used to build a genuinely close, real primary metric (6.25% margin) rather than the much more lopsided full-field composite the raw data alone would suggest (Seton Hall computes to ~6th-9th of 353 by a simple opponent-adjusted average, not a close call). This mirrors the cardiology precedent: pick the real metric that is actually close as primary_metric, disclose the lopsided one as real context driving other deliverables (D3/D4/D5). The legacy Guide Notes.docx found alongside the case materials is for an unrelated case ('College Admissions') -- not usable content; FACILITATOR.md's anchor ladder, twist, and Socratic questions below are authored fresh from case.md's own real data, per case-write SKILL.md step 5's instruction to author an original sound twist when the legacy materials don't supply one. A real, disclosed data-quality defect in the source workbook (83 of 353 win-loss records corrupted by spreadsheet auto-date-formatting, unrecoverable) is reported as NOT FOUND/CORRUPTED rather than guessed at (Appendix C).

balance.argument_a: Both real, independent rankings that existed the day the season stopped placed Seton Hall inside the top 16: final AP media poll No. 15, NCAA's own NET system also No. 15 (through games of March 12, 2020, the last date played). The case's own opponent-adjusted bubble-field composite (MA1) places Seton Hall 9th of 25, ahead of West Virginia, Penn St., Oklahoma, and Butler. A 21-9 record with a share of the Big East regular-season title and a top-12-nationally strength of schedule (Opp Rating Diff 11.48) is a genuine top-16 resume by essentially every credible measure available that day.
balance.argument_b: The AP margin is one spot (15 of a 16 cutoff) -- the thinnest possible edge -- and a media poll is a popularity/resume vote, not the committee's own opponent-adjusted formula. Stripped of opponent adjustment, Seton Hall's raw Team Offensive Rating rank (29th) and Team Defensive Rating rank (25th) are mediocre in isolation and land it in a virtual tie for 14th-15th within the bubble field -- right on the line. Judged on win-loss record alone (21-9, .700), Seton Hall trails nearly every other bubble-caliber team in Appendix B on losses. And unlike every conference-tournament team, Seton Hall never got the chance to add a signature March win; its resume is frozen incomplete.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric is Seton Hall's rank in the final AP media poll -- the last complete, dated national ranking before the season was suspended -- relative to the No. 16 cutoff: 15 vs. 16, a real, sourced, 6.25% margin ((16-15)/16). See derived{} for the full worked comparison against NET and the bubble-field composite.
balance.stability: NOT STABLE (Tier 2 P5 mechanical FAIL, 2026-08-13, cases/seton-hall/sensitivity_model.py). The verdict flips under a +50% flex of ap_rank (15 -> 22.5, rounds to 23): the case's own real, cited primary metric sits only 2 spots from the flip point (ap_rank=17). No stated Modeling Assumption (MA1-MA3) causes this -- MA1 does not touch the primary metric, MA2/MA3 are fixed external tournament rules, not author dials -- so the instability comes from how thin the real, cited AP-poll margin itself is, not from an assumption the case chose. Genuine elimination was attempted and rejected: switching the primary metric to NET rank would not remove the instability now that NET's corrected final value (No. 15, see sources[] S5 2026-08-18 correction) matches the AP margin exactly rather than offering a wider one -- the case was deliberately built around the AP margin because it is a real, directly-cited ranking (see legacy_conversion_note), and NET no longer offers an alternate wider-margin metric to swap to even if that had been desired. Per MCS-26/41, a disclosed-but-not-eliminated instability has no pass state: P5 is reported FAIL, matching the project's own flagship case (Cold Chain). Guide Notes 'Lessons Learned' carries the same disclosure -- a guide defending 'No. 15 of 16' as an unshakeable margin is defending a margin that would not survive the AP voters ranking Seton Hall two spots lower.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: ap_rank is a real, cited historical fact (S4), but it IS the graded primary metric itself, resting on the thinnest possible real margin (1 AP-poll spot of 16). Whether a bubble team's rank would have landed differently under slightly different voter behavior is inherently unknowable in advance -- a forecast-shaped question about a committee's judgment, not a research gap. Testing its fragility is the case's own point (see sensitivity_model.py's docstring).
